Foundations: Value, Trust and Account Health

High-value clients behave differently from one-off customers, and they carry different risks. In this module you measure how much your business depends on each client, learn a practical model of trust, and build a simple health score that warns you before a good account goes quiet.
High-value accounts: concentration risk and account tiers
Calculate what share of your monthly income each client provides
Explain concentration risk and what happens to your business if a large client leaves
Sort your clients into strategic, key and standard tiers
Decide how much time and attention each tier should receive

Most client advice is written for the first sale. This course is about what happens after. A **high-value account** is a client who pays you regularly, often on a monthly **retainer** (a fixed fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work), and whose loss would hurt your income. A social media manager with a monthly hospital contract, a bookkeeper serving three schools, or a caterer who supplies an office canteen every week all manage accounts like this.

Advanced client management has three jobs. First, **keep** the account by delivering reliably and communicating well. Second, **protect** it by spotting trouble early. Third, **grow** it through renewal at a fair price and, where it truly helps the client, extra work. Before any of that, you need to know which clients matter most to your business, in numbers, not feelings.
A woman studying charts that show money coming in
Start by looking at where your monthly income actually comes from, client by client.
Concentration risk

**Concentration risk** is the danger of depending on one or two clients for a large share of your income. A big client feels like good news, and it is, until that client changes manager, cuts budget or moves the work in-house. If one account pays most of your bills, losing it can force you to lay off staff or borrow. The cure is not to avoid big clients. It is to know your exposure, manage that account with extra care, and keep building other income so no single exit can sink you.
Worked example: one agency's exposure

For example, Ada runs a three-person digital marketing agency in Lagos with five retainer clients. Her monthly team and office costs are about N900,000. These are example figures for practice, not market prices.
She lists monthly fees: Client A N600,000, Client B N250,000, Client C N200,000, Client D N150,000, Client E N100,000.
She works out Client A's share: 600,000 divided by 1,300,000 = 0.46, so about 46% of her income.
She tests the worst case: without Client A, income falls to 1,300,000 minus 600,000 = N700,000, which is N200,000 below her N900,000 costs every month.
She works out Client A's yearly value: 600,000 x 12 = N7,200,000.

Ada now knows that one client carries nearly half her business. She decides to give Client A her most senior attention, set her own limit that no single client should exceed about a third of income, and spend two hours a week winning new work so that share falls over time.
Sorting clients into tiers

Not every client needs the same level of service. Giving everyone the same attention usually means your best clients get too little and your smallest get more than they pay for. A simple three-tier system helps you decide where your hours go. Use your own business numbers to set the boundaries.
Tier
Typical signs
Attention you give
Strategic
Large share of income, long contract, room to grow, senior contact
Owner or most senior person leads; monthly check-in; quarterly review; health score every month
Key
Steady monthly fee, good fit, some growth possible
Named account lead; fortnightly update; review twice a year
Standard
Small or occasional work, clear and simple scope
Efficient service, templates, update at each delivery
Account tiers
Strategic: few, highest value
Key: steady core accounts
Standard: many, simple scope
Few accounts sit at the top, but they deserve the most senior time and the closest watching.

Tiers are about service level, not respect. A standard client still deserves courtesy, honesty and on-time delivery. The difference is in how much proactive time you invest, such as strategy calls, reviews and extra ideas. Review tiers every quarter, because a standard client can grow into a key one, and a strategic one can shrink.
Do not let one client run your business

When a client knows they are most of your income, the pressure to say yes to everything grows: unpaid extras, late-night calls, delayed payments. Knowing your exposure helps you stay calm and professional, because you are already working on a plan B.
Where this skill is used

In companies, this work is called account management or client success. In agencies and consulting firms, a named account lead owns each large client. Freelancers and small business owners do the same job themselves. Remote clients, including clients abroad who pay through platforms or in foreign currency, need even more deliberate management, because you rarely meet in person and silence is easy to misread.
Keep: deliver what you promised, on time, and say so clearly.
Protect: watch for warning signs and act before the client complains.
Grow: renew on fair terms and offer extra work only when it serves the client's goals.

How trust is built: the Trust Equation and multi-threaded relationships
Name the four parts of the Trust Equation and what each one means
Score your own trustworthiness with a client and find the weakest part
Plan specific actions that raise reliability and lower self-orientation
Build relationships with more than one person inside a client organisation

Clients rarely leave because of one mistake. They leave when they stop trusting you. Trust can feel mysterious, but it can be broken down into parts you can work on. A useful model is the **Trust Equation**, first published in the book *The Trusted Advisor* (2000), co-written by David Maister, Charles H. Green and Robert Galford.
The four parts
Part
Question it answers
What it looks like with a client
Credibility
Can I believe what you say?
You know your field, give accurate answers and admit when you do not know
Reliability
Do you do what you said?
Reports arrive on the agreed day; you return calls when you said you would
Intimacy
Do I feel safe telling you things?
The client shares worries and bad news with you because you keep confidences and do not judge
Self-orientation
Whose interests are you focused on?
High when you push your own sales or talk about yourself; low when you listen and focus on the client's goals

The equation puts credibility, reliability and intimacy on top, added together, and self-orientation underneath. In words: **trust grows when the top three rise and falls when self-orientation rises.** Self-orientation is the one most people overlook. You can be skilled and punctual, but if the client senses you care more about the next invoice than about their results, trust drops.
Two professionals shaking hands across a table
A signed contract starts the relationship; trust is what keeps it going.
Worked example: scoring and fixing trust

For example, Ngozi is a bookkeeper who serves a private school in Abuja on a monthly retainer. The bursar has gone quiet. Ngozi does an honest self-check, giving each part a score from 1 (weak) to 10 (strong). This is a personal reflection tool, not an official test.
She scores herself: Credibility 7, Reliability 4 (two monthly reports were late), Intimacy 6, Self-orientation 5 (her last two calls were about adding payroll services).
She adds the top three: 7 + 4 + 6 = 17. She divides by self-orientation: 17 divided by 5 = 3.4.
Her weakest areas are clear: reliability, and too much selling.
She commits to sending reports on the 5th of every month and stops pitching new services until the school raises a need.
Three months later she rescores: Reliability 8, Self-orientation 3. The top three now add to 7 + 8 + 6 = 21, and 21 divided by 3 = 7.0.
The number itself is only a guide, but the exercise showed Ngozi exactly what to fix. Being on time and focusing on the school's problems did more for trust than any new service offer.
Self-oriented or client-oriented?
Self-oriented habits
Client-oriented habits
Talks about own achievements
Pitches extra services often
Defends quickly when criticised
Rushes to give the answer
Asks about client's goals first
Suggests work only when needed
Listens fully, then responds
Admits uncertainty honestly
Moving habits from the left column to the right lowers self-orientation, the denominator of the Trust Equation.
Practical ways to raise each part
Credibility: check facts before you send them, and say 'Let me confirm and come back to you by 3pm' instead of guessing.
Reliability: make small promises and keep them every time. Missed small promises add up faster than people expect.
Intimacy: keep what clients tell you private, remember what matters to them, and respond to bad news without blame.
Self-orientation: in every call, spend more time asking and listening than talking about yourself.
Do not rely on one contact

Many accounts are lost because the one person who liked you leaves the company. A **multi-threaded** relationship means you have good working links with several people at the client: the person who approves payment, the person you work with every day, and ideally someone senior who cares about the results. You build these links honestly, by copying the right people on reports they actually need, inviting the sponsor to quarterly reviews, and thanking colleagues who help.
Trust signals in remote relationships

With clients you rarely meet, such as a company in another state or abroad, trust is built almost entirely through small written and spoken signals. Answer within the time you agreed, even if only to say 'Received, I will reply fully by Thursday.' Turn on your camera for important video calls so the client sees a real person. Write updates that are short, specific and dated, so the client never has to chase you. When you are unsure of a time zone or a public holiday, ask, rather than assume.
Confirm every request in writing, even briefly.
Send bad news before the client finds it.
Use the client's name and refer to what they told you last time.
Keep personal opinions on politics and religion out of business chats.
Respect the main contact
Never go around your day-to-day contact to complain to their boss. Agree with your contact who should receive which updates, so wider relationships strengthen their position rather than threaten it.
Trust has four parts: credibility, reliability, intimacy and self-orientation.
High self-orientation, such as constant selling, can cancel out strong skills.
Small, kept promises are the fastest way to rebuild reliability.
Build honest working links with several people at each important client.

Building an account health score that warns you early

By the time a client says 'We have decided not to renew', the decision was usually made weeks earlier. The signs were there: slower replies, a new manager who never joined a call, invoices paid later than before. An **account health score** collects those signs into one number so you notice the pattern while there is still time to act.

Sponsor engagement

Sponsor has changed or never appears

Building a weighted score

Score each signal from 1 (very poor) to 5 (excellent) once a month. Because some signals matter more than others, give each one a **weight**, a percentage that shows its importance. The weights must add up to 100%. The weights below are a sensible starting point; adjust them to your business. Then multiply each score by its weight and add the results. The final number is out of 5.
Agree your weights, for example: delivery 25%, responsiveness 15%, satisfaction 25%, payment 20%, sponsor engagement 15%.
Score each signal from 1 to 5 using facts from the month, not your mood.
Multiply each score by its weight written as a decimal (25% is 0.25).
Add the five results to get a score out of 5.
Place the account in a band and take the matching action.
Worked example: scoring two accounts
For example, Ada from Lesson 1 scores two of her clients at the end of the month using the weights above.
Client A scores: delivery 4, responsiveness 3, satisfaction 2 (two complaints about post quality), payment 5, sponsor engagement 2 (new marketing director has not met Ada).
Client B scores: delivery 5, responsiveness 4, satisfaction 4, payment 3, sponsor 4.

Client B is green. Client A, her largest account, is amber at 3.25, even though it pays on time. Ada books a meeting with the new marketing director within two weeks and agrees a quality check on posts before they go out.

Watch the trend, not just the number
A score that drops from 4.4 to 3.6 over three months is more worrying than a steady 3.6. Keep a monthly history so you can see the direction.
Ask the client directly

Your score is your view. Balance it with the client's own view by asking one short question each month, at the end of your monthly report: 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied are you with our work this month, and what is one thing we could do better?' Use the answer as the satisfaction score. A client who gives a 3 and names a specific problem is giving you a gift: a clear thing to fix while the account is still yours. A client who stops answering this question is also telling you something, so lower the responsiveness score and pick up the phone.

Keep the score honest. If you score yourself kindly on delivery, the tool becomes useless. Use evidence: dates in your project tracker, payment dates from your bank or Moniepoint, Opay or Paystack records, and the client's own words in emails or WhatsApp messages. When you store these notes, remember they are about real people and businesses. Keep them in a password-protected file and do not share them outside your team.
Lost accounts usually show warning signs weeks before the client says so.

Onboarding, Retainer Control and Quarterly Reviews

Most problems with large clients start in the first month or creep in through unmanaged extra requests. This module gives you an onboarding kit with a communication charter and RACI chart, a method for tracking retainer hours and handling change requests, and a quarterly business review that shows the client the value they receive.
The onboarding kit: kickoff meeting, communication charter and RACI
Plan the first 30 days of a new high-value account
Run a kickoff meeting with a clear agenda
Write a communication charter covering channels, response times and escalation
Build a RACI chart so both sides know who does and decides what

The first month of a new account sets habits that last for years. If the client learns that you answer WhatsApp at 11pm, they will expect it. If nobody agrees who approves work, you will wait days for decisions and get blamed for delays. **Onboarding** is the planned process of starting a client relationship so that expectations are written down and agreed before the pressure of real deadlines begins.
A person being guided through the first steps of a new process
A planned onboarding turns a signed contract into a working relationship with clear rules.
The first 30 days
First 30 days of a new account
Day 0: contract signed
Days 1 to 3: kickoff
Week 1: access and assets
Week 2: first delivery
Day 30: onboarding review
Each stage has one job, ending with a review where both sides say what is and is not working.
The kickoff meeting

Hold a kickoff call or meeting within three working days of signing, with the main contact and, if possible, the sponsor who approved the budget. Send the agenda a day before. Cover: the client's goals for the next three to twelve months and how they will judge success; the agreed scope from the contract, read aloud in plain words; who is involved on both sides; how you will communicate; what you need from them (logins, brand files, data) and by when; and the date of the first delivery. Send written notes the same day and ask the client to confirm or correct them.
The communication charter

A **communication charter** is a short, agreed document that sets the rules for how you and the client talk. It protects both sides: the client knows when to expect answers, and you protect your evenings and weekends. Keep it to one page.
Item
Example wording
Channels
WhatsApp group for quick questions; email for approvals, invoices and anything that changes scope
Response times
Replies within 4 working hours, Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm; urgent issues by phone call
Regular updates
Written progress update every Friday by 3pm; monthly report by the 5th
Approvals
Client approves or comments within 2 working days; after that, the schedule moves
Escalation
If a problem is not solved by the account lead in 2 working days, it goes to the agency owner and the client's marketing manager
The RACI chart

Confusion about roles causes many client disputes. A **RACI chart** lists each recurring task and marks who is **R**esponsible (does the work), **A**ccountable (owns the result and makes the final decision), **C**onsulted (gives input before) and **I**nformed (is told after). Common guidance is to have exactly one Accountable person per task, so there is always one clear decision-maker.
Worked example: a RACI chart for a hospital social media retainer

For example, Ada's agency starts managing Facebook and Instagram for a private hospital in Ibadan. On the agency side are Ada (owner) and Tolu (content writer). On the client side are Bisi (marketing officer) and the medical director.
Monthly content calendar: Tolu is R, Ada is A, Bisi is C, the medical director is I.
Approval of any post with health information: Bisi is R, the medical director is A, Ada is C, Tolu is I.
Publishing approved posts: Tolu is R, Ada is A, Bisi is I.
Replying to patient comments: Bisi is R and A because only hospital staff may discuss patient matters; Ada is C on tone; Tolu is I.
Ada checks every row has exactly one A, then shares the chart at the kickoff for agreement.

Both teams now know that the medical director, not the agency, signs off health information, and that the hospital handles patient questions. This protects patients, the hospital and Ada's agency from a serious mistake.
Access and client data

Never ask for a client's personal passwords. Ask to be added with your own login or partner access, which most business platforms provide, so access can be removed when the work ends. Keep client and customer data private and use it only for the agreed work. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, sets rules for handling personal data.
The client inputs list

Many first deliveries are late because the provider is waiting for things from the client. At kickoff, agree a written list of inputs with an owner and a due date for each: logo and brand colours, product price list, access to the social media pages, previous reports, and the names of anyone who must approve work. Track the list in your weekly update. If an input is late, say so politely and show the effect on the schedule, so a delay is never blamed on you by default.
Send the charter and RACI with the kickoff notes and ask for written agreement.
Pin the charter in the WhatsApp group so new members see it.
At the Day 30 review, ask: what should we start, stop or keep doing?
Agree expectations in writing before real deadlines start.

Retainer control: tracking hours, preventing scope creep and change requests
Calculate the effective hourly rate of a retainer
Track hours used against hours included and project the month-end total
Tell the difference between in-scope work and a change request
Handle a change request in writing with an estimate and clear choices

A **retainer** is a fixed monthly fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work, such as 30 hours of marketing support or 12 social media posts. Retainers are good for both sides: the client gets steady service, and you get predictable income. They also carry a quiet danger: **scope creep**, where small extra requests pile up until you are doing far more work for the same fee. Scope creep rarely comes from bad clients. It comes from unclear scope and nobody tracking the hours.
A person organising tasks on a large schedule board
Tracking hours against the retainer every week shows trouble before the month is over.
Know your effective rate

Divide the monthly fee by the hours included to get your **effective hourly rate**. This is the number you use to price extra work and to see whether an account is profitable. If you regularly work more hours than included, your real rate falls without anyone noticing.
Worked example: a month that is running over

For example, Halima's agency has a retainer with a school: N450,000 a month for 30 hours of marketing work. These are example figures. It is day 15 of a 30-day month and her time log shows 21 hours used.
Effective rate: 450,000 divided by 30 hours = N15,000 per hour.
Hours used so far: 21 out of 30, which is 70% of the hours with only 50% of the month gone.
Projected month total: 21 hours divided by 15 days, times 30 days = 42 hours.
Projected overrun: 42 minus 30 = 12 hours. At N15,000 per hour, that is 12 x 15,000 = N180,000 of unpaid work.
She checks the log: 9 of the 21 hours went on a new admissions landing page that was never in the scope.
Halima now has facts, not a feeling. She treats the landing page as a change request, and she shares the hours summary with the school before the overrun happens, not after.
In scope or a change request?
In scope (part of the retainer)
Change request (extra, needs approval)
Work listed in the contract, such as 12 posts a month
New deliverables, such as a website page or a video
Normal revisions agreed in the contract, such as two rounds
A fourth or fifth round of revisions after approval
Monthly report in the agreed format
A new report for the board in a different format
Work within agreed hours
Rush work outside agreed working hours
Handling a change request
Client asks for extra
Log the request
Estimate hours and cost
Client chooses an option
Schedule and confirm in writing
Every extra request follows the same path, so nothing is done for free by accident.
Giving the client choices

Do not answer an extra request with a flat 'no' or a silent 'yes'. Thank the client, estimate the work and offer clear options. For the landing page, Halima estimates 10 hours. She writes by email: 'Thank you for the landing page request. It is outside our monthly scope. We estimate 10 hours, which is N150,000 at our retainer rate. You can: (1) approve it as extra work, invoiced separately; (2) swap it for 10 hours of this month's planned work, which would move the March newsletter to April; or (3) schedule it for next month within the normal hours.' The client chooses, and the choice is recorded.
Log time daily against each client and task, using a simple sheet or a free time-tracking app.
Every Friday, compare hours used with hours included and project the month-end total.
At 75% of hours used, tell the client and agree priorities for the rest of the month.
Send a short monthly hours summary with the report so the client sees what the fee bought.
Write scope so it can be measured

Most scope creep starts with vague words in the agreement, such as 'social media support' or 'reasonable revisions'. Replace them with countable terms: '12 posts per month across Facebook and Instagram', 'up to two rounds of revisions per post', 'replies within 4 working hours, Monday to Friday', 'work requested after 5pm on Friday starts on Monday'. Also list what is not included, for example paid advertising budgets, printing or photography. Clear scope does not make you rigid. It gives you and the client a shared reference point, so a conversation about extra work feels fair rather than personal.
Deliverable-based retainers

If your retainer counts deliverables, such as 12 posts, rather than hours, the same method works. Track deliverables and revision rounds used against those included, and still log hours privately so you know your real effective rate for each client.
Small favours still count

It is fine to do a five-minute favour for a good client, but log it and mention it: 'We added the extra caption at no charge this time.' The client sees your goodwill, and you keep a record if favours start to grow.
Effective hourly rate equals the monthly fee divided by the hours included.
Project the month-end hours at mid-month so you can act before an overrun.
New deliverables, extra revision rounds and rush work are change requests.
Answer extra requests with an estimate and clear options, confirmed in writing.

Running a quarterly business review that proves your value
Explain the purpose of a quarterly business review (QBR)
Prepare a results summary that compares outcomes with agreed goals
Present results honestly, separating what you caused from what you contributed to
Run a 60-minute QBR agenda and agree next-quarter goals

Weekly updates show activity. A **quarterly business review (QBR)** steps back to answer the questions a sponsor really asks: Are we getting results for our money? What did we learn? What should we do next? It is held every three months with your main contact and the sponsor. Done well, it is the single strongest tool for renewal, because the client hears your value from you before they hear a cheaper offer from someone else.
A woman presenting results on a screen to colleagues
A QBR is a short, honest presentation of results against the goals agreed at kickoff.
Prepare the results summary

Go back to the goals agreed at kickoff and report against them, not against whatever looks good. Use the client's own data where possible, such as orders from their sales records. Show the goal, the actual result and the difference. Then add two or three lessons learned and the risks you see coming.
Worked example: a bakery's online orders

For example, Ada's agency runs online marketing for a bakery in Port Harcourt on a N450,000 monthly retainer. The goal agreed at kickoff was 600 online orders in the quarter. The bakery's own order records are used. These are example figures.
Actual online orders: 690. Against the goal: 690 divided by 600 = 1.15, so 115% of target.
Average order value from the bakery's records: N8,500. Online order revenue: 690 x 8,500 = N5,865,000.
Agency fees for the quarter: 3 x 450,000 = N1,350,000.
Revenue from online orders is about 5,865,000 divided by 1,350,000 = 4.3 times the fee.
Ada adds an honest note: some of these orders would have come anyway from loyal customers, so the agency contributed to this revenue but did not cause all of it.
The bakery owner sees clear progress against the agreed goal and trusts the numbers more because Ada did not claim credit for every naira. They agree a new goal of 750 orders for next quarter.
Never inflate results

Do not present guesses as facts, hide a missed target, or claim all of a client's growth. If a target was missed, say so, explain why and present your plan. Sponsors often check numbers, and one inflated claim can undo a year of trust.

Listen more than you present

Give the client's priorities as much time as your results. Ask open questions such as: 'What has changed in your business since we last met?', 'What will your board or owner judge you on this year?' and 'What would make the next quarter a success for you personally?' Their answers feed the renewal and growth conversations in Module 3. Write them down in their own words.
Choosing the right measures

Report two kinds of measures. **Outcome measures** show what the client cares about, such as orders, enquiries, enrolments or money saved. **Activity measures** show what you did, such as posts published or reports filed. Lead with outcomes, because the sponsor is paying for results, and use activity measures to explain them. Choose no more than five measures in total, and keep the same ones each quarter so the client can compare.
When results are poor

Do not cancel or delay a QBR because the numbers are weak. A review held in a bad quarter often builds more trust than one held in a good quarter, because the client sees you face the facts. Show the shortfall, give your honest analysis of the causes, separate causes you control from those you do not, and bring a specific recovery plan with dates. Ask the client what they think went wrong; they often know things you do not.
Keep a goals register
Keep one page per client listing every goal agreed at kickoff and each QBR, with dates. It stops goals from quietly changing and makes the next review quick to prepare.
Send a short pre-read two days before, so the meeting is for discussion, not reading slides.

Difficult Moments, Renewal and Your Client Playbook

Strong accounts are tested when something goes wrong, when a contract comes up for renewal, and when the person managing it changes. This module covers service recovery conversations, renewal and fair price adjustments, measuring growth across your client base, and the handover and reflection that complete your Client Relationship Management Playbook.
Delivering bad news and recovering from service failures
Prepare for a difficult client conversation using facts, impact and options
Deliver bad news early, by voice, and take clear ownership
Decide a fair, proportionate remedy and calculate its cost
Respond professionally when a client is angry or when the client is at fault

Every long client relationship includes failures: a missed deadline, a wrong figure in a report, a post that offended customers. Clients usually forgive a mistake. What they find hard to forgive is hearing about it late, hearing excuses, or discovering it themselves. How you handle a failure can leave the relationship weaker or, surprisingly often, stronger than before.
A professional on a phone call at her desk
Serious bad news belongs in a call, not a text message, followed by a written summary.
Before the conversation
Facts: what happened, when, and what is affected. Check them twice.
Cause: your honest understanding of why it happened, without blaming staff by name.
Impact on the client: what this means for their business, customers or reputation.
Options: two or three ways forward, with your recommendation.
Remedy: what you will do to make it right and to stop it happening again.
A service recovery conversation
Tell them early
Own it plainly
Explain impact
Offer options and remedy
Confirm in writing
Speed and ownership come first; options and the written follow-up turn an apology into a plan.
During the conversation

Call as soon as you know, even before you have every answer. Open plainly: 'I need to tell you about a problem with the admissions campaign. It is our mistake.' Avoid long explanations at the start; the client wants to know what happened and what it means. Then listen. Let the client react without interrupting or defending. Summarise what you heard, present your options, agree the next step and say when you will update them again. Within the same day, send an email confirming what was agreed.
Worked example: a late campaign launch

For example, Ada's agency promised to launch a school's admissions campaign on 1 March. A design error meant it went live five days late. The school pays a N450,000 monthly retainer at an effective rate of N15,000 per hour. These are example figures.
Ada calls the head of admissions on the morning she learns of the delay, not after launch.
She owns it: 'We did not check the final design in time. That is our failure.' She explains the impact: five fewer days of enquiries before the open day.
She offers options: (1) extend the campaign by five days at no cost; (2) add a free reminder post series in the week before the open day.
She proposes a remedy: four hours of extra work at no charge, worth 4 x 15,000 = N60,000.
She checks proportion: 60,000 divided by 450,000 = 0.133, about 13% of one month's fee, a meaningful gesture that the agency can afford.
She explains the prevention step: a second person now checks every final design two days before launch.
The school accepts the extension and the extra posts. At the next quarterly review, the head of admissions mentions that the agency's honesty about the delay was a reason to keep working together.
Remedies should fit the harm

A remedy is not a bribe. Offer something proportionate that repairs the actual damage, such as extra work or extended time, rather than a large discount that teaches the client to expect money every time something goes wrong. Never promise a remedy you cannot deliver.
When the client is angry

Stay calm and lower your voice rather than raising it. Acknowledge the feeling without accepting false facts: 'I can hear how frustrating this is.' Ask for time if you need to check something: 'Let me confirm the dates and call you back by 2pm.' If the client becomes abusive or threatening, you may end the call politely, write down what happened and involve your manager or the client's senior contact. Professional does not mean accepting abuse.
When the client is at fault

Sometimes the delay is theirs: approvals took a week, or content arrived late. Do not blame, but do not take the blame either. Point to the agreement calmly: 'Our charter allows two working days for approvals. The posts were approved on day six, so the launch moves to the 12th. Would you like us to prioritise anything to help?' This is why the communication charter and RACI chart from Module 2 matter: they turn arguments into facts.
After any failure, hold a short internal review within a week: what happened, why, and what process change prevents it.
Record the failure and the remedy in the client's file so the next account lead knows the history.
Check the account's health score the following month to see whether trust has recovered.
Data mistakes are serious

If a failure involves personal data, such as a customer list sent to the wrong person, tell the client immediately so they can meet their own legal duties. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets obligations for handling personal data and for responding to breaches.
Tell the client early, by voice, and own the mistake in plain words.
Prepare facts, impact, options and a remedy before you call.
Make remedies proportionate to the harm and follow up in writing.
When the client is at fault, refer calmly to the agreed charter rather than blaming.

Renewals, fair price adjustments and measuring account growth
Plan a renewal timeline that starts 90 days before a contract ends
Calculate and justify a price adjustment and its yearly effect
Propose expansion only when it serves a goal the client has stated
Calculate net revenue retention for your client base

Many service providers treat renewal as paperwork that happens in the last week of a contract. By then it is too late to fix problems, the client's budget for next year may already be set, and a competitor may have been talking to them for months. Advanced account managers treat renewal as a planned process that starts well before the end date.
A signed contract with a check mark
A renewal is earned through the year and confirmed on paper at the end.
Renewal timeline
90 days: review health and results
60 days: renewal conversation
45 days: written proposal
30 days: agree terms
0 days: new contract starts
Starting at 90 days leaves time to fix issues and fit the client's budget cycle.
Preparing the renewal conversation

At 90 days, look at the account's health score history, the QBR notes and the hours log. Ask yourself honestly: did we meet the goals, is this account profitable, and what does the client want next year? At 60 days, have a direct conversation: 'Our agreement ends on 31 December. Before I prepare a proposal, I would like to understand your plans for next year and anything you would like us to change.' Clients expect this conversation; avoiding it can look like you are unsure of your value.
Adjusting your price fairly

Your costs rise over time: data, fuel for generators, staff salaries, software subscriptions. If you never adjust prices, your profit on long accounts shrinks each year. A fair adjustment is explained with reasons, given with notice, and linked to value. Base the size of your adjustment on your actual cost increases and the results delivered, not on a figure copied from elsewhere.
Worked example: a 12% retainer adjustment

For example, Halima's school retainer is N450,000 a month. Her data, power and staff costs for this account have risen over the year, and the school met its enquiry goals. She proposes a 12% adjustment at renewal. These are example figures.
New monthly fee: 450,000 x 1.12 = N504,000.
Old yearly value: 450,000 x 12 = N5,400,000. New yearly value: 504,000 x 12 = N6,048,000.
Yearly difference: 6,048,000 minus 5,400,000 = N648,000.
She writes the reasons in the proposal: rising delivery costs, goals met, and one added service (a monthly parents' newsletter) that the school asked for at the QBR.
She offers a choice: the full service at N504,000, or the current scope without the newsletter at a smaller adjustment.
The school chooses the full service. Because Halima raised the subject at 60 days with clear reasons and a choice, the bursar could fit it into next year's budget.
Expansion that serves the client

**Expansion** means a client buying more from you: more hours, a new service or a new branch. Good expansion starts from something the client said, usually at a QBR: 'We are opening a second branch in June' or 'Our parents complain they never hear from us.' Link your proposal to that statement in their words. If you cannot connect an offer to a stated goal, it is probably self-oriented selling, which lowers trust.
Measuring growth across all clients

**Net revenue retention (NRR)** shows whether your existing clients, taken together, are paying you more or less than a year ago. It ignores new clients, so it measures account management, not sales. Formula: (starting monthly revenue + expansion minus reductions minus lost clients) divided by starting monthly revenue, times 100. Above 100% means your existing accounts grew overall.
Item (monthly, example)
Amount
Starting monthly revenue from existing clients
Expansion: Client B added a service
Reduction: Client D cut its scope
minus N50,000
Lost: Client E did not renew
minus N100,000
Result: 1,400,000 divided by 1,300,000
about 107.7%
When the client pushes back

Some clients will ask you to keep the old price or to cut it. Listen first and ask why: a tight budget, a cheaper quote, or doubt about value each need a different answer. If the budget is tight, offer a smaller scope at a fair price rather than the same work for less, because discounting the same work lowers your effective hourly rate for the whole year. If they have a cheaper quote, remind them of the results in your QBR and the cost of switching, without criticising the competitor. If they doubt the value, that is a warning sign you missed earlier; agree clear goals for the next quarter. Know in advance the lowest fee at which the account is still worth keeping.
Read NRR with your health scores
An NRR above 100% can still hide risk if most growth came from one client. Check concentration from Module 1 at the same time.

Write a handover note that lets a colleague take over an account without losing trust
Plan a joint introduction and an overlap period for a handover
Write an honest reflection on a relationship challenge using the STAR structure
Assemble the three parts of your Client Relationship Management Playbook

Accounts are often lost at the moment the account manager changes. The new person does not know the history, repeats questions the client has answered many times, and misses promises made by the last person. Whether you are leaving a role, going on maternity leave or giving an account to a team member as you grow, a planned handover protects the client and your reputation.
A stack of checked documents ready to hand over
A complete handover file means the client never has to explain their history twice.
What goes in a handover note
Account handover checklist
Contract, scope and renewal date
People, roles and RACI
Open promises and deadlines
Health score and history
Access transferred securely
Joint introduction held
Tick every item before the outgoing manager steps away from the account.

Write the note so a capable stranger could run the account tomorrow. Include the client's goals in their own words, sensitive topics to handle carefully (for example, a past dispute that was resolved), the communication charter, the last QBR notes and any change requests in progress. Transfer platform access by adding the new person's own login and removing the old one; never pass passwords along in a WhatsApp message.
Worked example: handing over three accounts
For example, Ada's senior account manager, Kemi, is leaving after giving a month's notice. Kemi manages Clients A, B and C, worth N600,000, N250,000 and N200,000 a month. These are example figures.
Because Client A is strategic and amber on its health score, Ada takes it herself; Tolu takes B and C.
Kemi writes one handover note per client using the checklist, and Ada reviews each one within two days.
In week 2, Kemi and the new lead hold a joint call with each client. Kemi introduces the new lead and confirms every open promise.
For the next two weeks the new lead runs the account while Kemi is still available for questions; after that, Kemi's access is removed.
All three clients renew at year end. Client A's sponsor later says the joint call made the change feel planned rather than sudden.
Reflecting honestly on a challenge

Employers and clients are more impressed by honest reflection on a hard situation than by stories where everything went perfectly. Use the **STAR** structure: **Situation** (the context), **Task** (what you were responsible for), **Action** (what you actually did) and **Result** (what happened, with numbers where possible). Then add a fifth part: **what I would do differently**. Remove client names and any confidential details, or ask permission before sharing.
STAR part
Example notes
Situation
A school client's new bursar questioned our retainer two months before renewal
Task
As account lead, I had to keep the account and rebuild trust with the new decision-maker
I requested a meeting, prepared a QBR with goals and results, and listened to her concerns about reporting
Result
The school renewed with a simpler monthly report; the account health score rose from 3.1 to 4.0 over two quarters
Do differently
Meet any new decision-maker within the first two weeks, not wait for them to raise concerns
Your Client Relationship Management Playbook

Your capstone brings this course together into a playbook you can reuse with every important client. It has three parts: an onboarding communication template (kickoff agenda, communication charter and RACI from Module 2), a documented relationship challenge (your STAR reflection, plus the recovery script from Lesson 1 of this module if relevant) and a proactive check-in and renewal plan (health score routine, QBR dates, renewal timeline and feedback questions).
When you receive an account

If you are the person taking over, read everything before you speak to the client: the contract, the charter, the last three reports, the QBR notes and the health score history. In your first call, do not ask questions the client has already answered in writing. Instead say what you understand and ask them to correct you: 'I understand your main goal this year is the second branch launch in June. Is that still right?' Keep every promise the previous manager made, even small ones, or explain clearly and early if one cannot be kept.
Read the full file before the first call.
Confirm goals and open promises in your own words.
Send a short note after the call listing what you will do and by when.
Tell clients early
Tell important clients about a change of account manager as soon as the decision is final, ideally before the outgoing person announces it elsewhere.
Keep it alive
Review the playbook every quarter. Add what you learn from each QBR, renewal and difficult moment, so it becomes your own working method rather than a document you wrote once.
A planned handover with a joint introduction protects accounts when people change.
Never pass passwords on; give new people their own access and remove old access.
STAR plus 'what I would do differently' makes an honest, credible reflection.

Why this matters
Keep, protect and grow
A high-value account pays you regularly
Keep: deliver on time, communicate well
Protect: spot trouble early
Grow: renew fairly, add work that helps
A high-value account is a client who pays you regularly, often on a monthly retainer, and whose loss would hurt your income.
A retainer is a fixed fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work.
Managing these clients has three jobs. First, keep the account, by delivering reliably and communicating well.
Second, protect it, by spotting trouble before the client complains.
Third, grow it, through renewal at a fair price and extra work only where it truly helps the client.
But first, you need to know which clients matter most, in numbers, not feelings.
Worked example
How much does one client carry?
For example, Ada runs a three-person agency in Lagos with five retainer clients.
Client A
Client B
Client C
Client D
Client E
Example figures for practice, not market prices.
Here is a worked example. Ada runs a three-person digital marketing agency in Lagos. Her monthly team and office costs are about 900,000 naira.
She lists each client's monthly fee. Client A pays 600,000 naira, Client B 250,000, Client C 200,000, and Clients D and E 150,000 and 100,000.
Together that is 1,300,000 naira a month.
Client A's share is 600,000 divided by 1,300,000, which is about 46% of her income.
Without Client A, income falls to 700,000 naira, which is 200,000 below her costs every month.
Match your time to the tier
Large share of income, room to grow. Senior lead, monthly check-in, quarterly review.
Steady monthly fee, good fit. Named account lead, fortnightly update, review twice a year.
Small or occasional work, simple scope. Efficient service, templates, update at each delivery.
That risk is called concentration risk: depending on one or two clients for a large share of your income. The cure is not to avoid big clients. It is to manage them with extra care.
Strategic clients get the owner or most senior person, a monthly check-in, and a quarterly review.
Key clients pay a steady monthly fee. They get a named account lead, an update every two weeks, and a review twice a year.
Standard clients get efficient service and an update at each delivery.
Tiers are about service level, not respect. Every client still deserves courtesy and on-time delivery. Review tiers every quarter.
The Trust Equation
The four parts of trust
Credibility: can I believe what you say?
Reliability: do you do what you said?
Intimacy: do I feel safe telling you things?
Self-orientation: whose interests come first?
Clients rarely leave because of one mistake. They leave when they stop trusting you. The Trust Equation breaks trust into four parts.
Credibility: you know your field and admit when you do not know.
Reliability: reports arrive on the agreed day, and you call back when you said you would.
Intimacy: the client shares worries with you because you keep confidences and do not judge.
Self-orientation sits underneath the other three. When you push your own sales, it rises and trust falls.
For example, Ngozi, a bookkeeper, scored her reliability 4 after two late reports. She sent reports on the 5th of every month and stopped pitching, and her trust score rose from 3.4 to 7.0.

Lost accounts usually show warning signs weeks before the client says so. A health score collects those signs into one number.
Once a month, score five signals from 1, very poor, to 5, excellent.
The signals are your delivery, the client's responsiveness, their satisfaction, how they pay, and whether the sponsor, the decision-maker, stays engaged.
Give each a weight that adds to 100%, for example delivery 25%, responsiveness 15%, satisfaction 25%, payment 20% and sponsor 15%. Multiply each score by its weight and add.
Ada's Client A scored 3.25 out of 5. That is amber, even though it pays on time, because a new marketing director had never met her.
Use evidence: delivery dates, payment records and the client's own words. A score that drops from 4.4 to 3.6 over three months is more worrying than a steady 3.6.
Common mistake
Risky
One person who likes you
Constant selling
Scoring yourself kindly
Safer
Links with several people
Listen more than you talk
Score with dates and records
Many accounts are lost because the one person who liked you leaves the company.
Build honest links with the person who approves payment, the person you work with daily, and someone senior who cares about results. Never go around your main contact to complain to their boss.
Key points
Remember
Work out each client's share of your income
Sort clients into strategic, key and standard
Trust falls when self-orientation rises
Score account health monthly and act on amber
To remember. Know each client's share of your income. Match your time to the tier. Keep small promises and sell less. And score account health every month, acting quickly on amber or red.

Start right, control the retainer, prove your value
Start right, control the retainer, and prove your value.
This is the video for module two of Advanced Client Management.
Why this matters
Most problems start in month one
The first month sets habits for years
Write expectations down early
Track hours before they run over
Show the value the client receives
The first month of a new account sets habits that last for years. If the client learns that you answer WhatsApp at 11pm, they will expect it.
Onboarding is the planned start of a client relationship, so that expectations are written down and agreed before real deadlines begin.
In this module you build an onboarding kit, learn to control a retainer, and run a quarterly review that shows the client what they get for their money.
The onboarding kit
Three tools for a clean start
Within three working days of signing. Goals, scope, people, communication, client inputs, first delivery.
One page: channels, response times, update days, approvals and escalation.
Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. Exactly one Accountable per task.

First, hold a kickoff meeting within three working days of signing. Cover the client's goals, the agreed scope in plain words, who is involved, how you will communicate, what you need from them and by when, and the first delivery date.
Send written notes the same day.

Second, a communication charter. For example: replies within 4 working hours, Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm, and the client approves work within 2 working days. It protects your evenings, and the client knows when to expect answers.
Third, a RACI chart. For each task, it names who does the work, who owns the final decision, who gives input first, and who is told after.
In Ada's hospital account, the medical director, not the agency, signs off any post with health information.
Protect client data
Access the safe way
Never
Ask for personal passwords
Use client data for other work
Always
Get your own login or partner access
Keep client data private
A word on safety. Never ask for a client's personal passwords.

Ask to be added with your own login, so access can be removed when the work ends. Keep client data private and use it only for the agreed work. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data.
Worked example
A retainer running over
For example, Halima's agency has a school retainer: 30 hours of marketing work a month.
Monthly fee
Effective rate per hour
Unpaid work if 12 hours over
Example figures, not market prices.
A retainer is a fixed monthly fee for agreed ongoing work. Its quiet danger is scope creep, where small extra requests pile up until you do far more work for the same fee.
Halima's agency has a school retainer for 30 hours a month.
The fee is 450,000 naira. Divide it by 30 hours, and her effective hourly rate is 15,000 naira.
On day 15, her log shows 21 hours used. At that pace she will reach 42 hours, which is 12 hours over, or 180,000 naira of unpaid work.
The log shows 9 of those hours went on a landing page that was never in the scope.
Step by step
Handle a change request
Offer the client clear options
Never a flat no, never a silent yes.
New deliverables, extra revision rounds and rush work are change requests. First, log the request.
Then estimate it. Halima estimates 10 hours, which is 150,000 naira at her retainer rate.
Offer choices: approve it as extra work, swap it for 10 hours of planned work, or schedule it for next month.
The client chooses, and you record the choice in writing. Track hours every Friday, and when 75% of hours are used, tell the client and agree priorities.
Quarterly review
A 60-minute QBR
Results against the goals agreed
Next quarter plan and actions
Every three months, hold a quarterly business review with your contact and the sponsor. Report against the goals agreed at kickoff, using the client's own data.
Ada's bakery client set a goal of 600 online orders. They got 690, which is 115% of target.
Then share what worked and what did not. Ada added an honest note: some orders would have come anyway from loyal customers.
Give their priorities as much time as your results. Ask what has changed in their business.
Close by agreeing two or three goals for next quarter, with owners and the next review date.
Never inflate results. One inflated claim can undo a year of trust.
Key points
Remember
Agree charter and RACI before deadlines start
Effective rate is fee divided by hours
Answer extra requests with options in writing
Report results honestly against agreed goals

To remember. Write expectations down in the first month. Know your effective rate. Treat extra work as a change request with clear options. And in every quarterly review, report honestly against the goals you agreed.

Bad news, renewals and handovers done well
Bad news, renewals, and handovers done well.
This is the video for module three of Advanced Client Management.
Why this matters
Where strong accounts are tested
When something goes wrong
When the contract comes up for renewal
When the account manager changes
Every long client relationship includes failures. Clients usually forgive a mistake. What they find hard to forgive is hearing about it late, hearing excuses, or discovering it themselves.
Strong accounts are also tested at renewal, when the client decides whether to keep paying you.
And they are tested when the person managing them changes. This module shows you how to handle all three.
Service recovery
Deliver bad news well
Tell them early, by voice
Explain the impact
Offer options and a remedy
Confirm in writing the same day
A remedy should fit the harm. It is not a bribe.
Before you call, prepare the facts, the cause, the impact on the client, two or three options and a remedy. Then call as soon as you know. Serious bad news belongs in a call, not a text message.
Open plainly: I need to tell you about a problem. It is our mistake. Do not blame staff by name.
Explain what it means for their business, then listen without interrupting or defending.
Present your options, agree the next step, and say when you will update them again.
Within the same day, send an email confirming what was agreed. Offer something that repairs the actual damage, such as extra work or extended time, rather than a large discount.
Worked example
A late campaign launch
For example, Ada's agency launched a school's admissions campaign five days late.
Monthly retainer
Free extra work: 4 hours
Example figures, not market prices.
Here is a worked example. A design error meant a school's campaign went live five days late. Ada called the head of admissions the morning she learned of it, and said: that is our failure.
She offered to extend the campaign by five days at no cost, plus four hours of extra work, worth 60,000 naira at her rate of 15,000 an hour.
That is about 13% of one month's 450,000 naira fee: meaningful, and affordable.
Now a second person checks every final design two days before launch.
Hard calls
Angry client, or client at fault?
Client is angry
Stay calm, lower your voice
Acknowledge the feeling
Ask for time to check facts
Client is at fault
Do not blame, do not take blame
Point calmly to the charter
Give the new date, offer help

When a client is angry, stay calm and acknowledge the feeling without accepting false facts. If a client becomes abusive or threatening, you may end the call politely and involve your manager. Professional does not mean accepting abuse.
When the delay is theirs, point calmly to the agreement. For example: our charter allows two working days for approvals, so the launch moves. Would you like us to prioritise anything?
Start renewal 90 days early
Do not treat renewal as paperwork in the last week. At 90 days, review the health score history, quarterly review notes and hours log.
At 60 days, ask directly about the client's plans for next year and anything they want changed.
Send a written proposal at 45 days, and agree terms by 30 days. This gives time to fix problems and fit the client's budget.
A fair 12% adjustment
For example, Halima's school retainer is 450,000 naira a month, and her costs have risen.
New monthly fee
Old yearly value
New yearly value
Yearly difference. Example figures.
Your costs rise over time: data, fuel for generators, salaries. A fair price adjustment is explained with reasons, given with notice, and linked to value.
Halima proposes 12%. The new fee is 504,000 naira a month, and the yearly value rises from 5,400,000 to 6,048,000 naira.
That is a yearly difference of 648,000 naira.
She gave reasons, offered a choice of a smaller scope at a smaller adjustment, and the school chose the full service.
Handover
Before the old manager steps away
Accounts are often lost when the account manager changes. Write a handover note so a capable stranger could run the account tomorrow, and tick every item here.
Give the new person their own login and remove the old access. Never pass passwords on in a WhatsApp message.
Then hold a joint call so the client meets the new lead.
Key points
Remember
Tell bad news early, by voice, and own it
Make remedies fit the harm
Start renewal work 90 days before the end
Hand over with a note and a joint call

To remember. Tell bad news early and own it. Keep remedies proportionate. Start renewal 90 days before the contract ends, with clear reasons for any price change. And hand over accounts with a full note and a joint introduction.
